full_judgment:
10. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali in reply to the submissions of Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan has submitted that even if it is conceded for argument's sake that Bhupal Chandra Majumder was in the joint family with his other brothers, there was no legal bar in acquiring property individually by his personal income and the property as described in schedule-'1' to the plaint gifted to the defendant having been purchased by him his own money he rightly transferred the same to the defendant by the deed in question. He has further submitted that there is no presumption in law that a family, because it is joint possesses joint property or any property. He has lastly submitted that the burden of proof that any particular property is joint family property, is in the first instance upon the person who claims it as coparcenery (coparceners) property and in the instant case, the plaintiff having failed to discharge the said onus, the Appellate Court rightly dismissed the suit, the High Court Division was absolutely in error in interfering with the decree of the Appellate Court, the last Court of fact. In support of his submission, he has referred the cases of Mudigowda Gowdappa Sankh and others-Vs-Ramchandra Revgowda Sankh (dead) by his legal representatives and another, AIR 1969 SC 1076; Srecmati Aroti Rani Paul-Vs-Sree Sudarshan Kumar Paul and others, 2005(XIII) BLT (AD) 36 (also reported in 11 MLR (AD) 2006, 43) and Mahesh Chandra Das Chowdhury-Vs-Mukunda Chandra Das and others, 14 DLR 348. 

 15. In view of the converse submission of the learned Counsel of the respective party, we have gone through the evidence and we found that the witnesses clearly supported the case of the defendant that the deed in question was executed and registered by Bhupal Chandra Majumder and that the plaintiff failed to prove that the same was executed and registered through forgery and false personation (persona ion), but the High Court Division on a wrong approach of the case without considering the pleading of the plaintiff, the evidence adduced in the suit in a very casual manner just restored those of the trial Court. The High Court Division did not at all reverse the finding of the Appellate Court as to the execution and registration of the deed in question by Bhupal Chandra Majumder. The High Court Division also misread the judgment of the Appellate Court as it observed that the Appellate Court sifted only one witness, the D.W.6 out of 10 witnesses, remaining quite silent about the statement of 4 PWs and 5 DWs" whereas, on a reading of the judgment of the Appellate Court, it is clear that it discussed and sifted all the material evidence including those of DW 6 in coming to the finding that the deed in question was executed and registered by Bhupal Chandra Majumder. The High Court Division also failed to consider that the deed in question being a registered one, it had a presumption of correctness under clause (e) of section 114 of the Evidence Act and that since the plaintiff asserted the same to have been created through forgery and false personation, onus was squarely upon him to prove the said allegation, but he failed to discharge the said onus. 

 "....there is no presumption that a Hindu family merely because it is joint, possesses any joint property. The burden of proving that any particular property is joint family property is, therefore, in the first instance upon the person who claims it as coparcenry (coparcener) property. But if the possession of a nucleus of the joint family property is either admitted or proved, any acquisition made by a member of the joint family is presumed to be joint family property. This is however subject to the limitation that the joint family property must be such as with its aid the property in question could have been acquired. It is only after the possession of an adequate nucleus is shown, that the onus shifts on to the person who claims the property as self-acquisition to affirmatively make out that the property was acquired without any aid from the family estate." 

 21. Similar view was taken in the case of Mahesh Chandra Das Chowdhury (supra) "... In Hindu law there is no presumption that a family, because it is joint possesses joint property or any property. When a property stands in the name of one member of a Hindu joint family, in order to render that property joint the other members of that family must prove that the family was possessed of some property with the income of which the property in question could have been acquired or that it was purchased with joint family funds, or by joint labour. In other words, in order to render such property as appertaining to the Hindu joint family it shall be necessary to establish the existence of at least such a nucleus of joint family property as is sufficient to yield an income with which that property could be acquired (Sections 233 and 286 of Mulla's Hindu Law, 10th edition may be referred to). Thus, the learned Subordinate Judge was not correct in presuming that the suit land was the joint family property merely because there existed a Hindu joint family. Under the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law by which the parties are admittedly governed, every member of a Hindu joint family takes a defined share of the joint property and is competent to alienate his share." 

 24. Relevant portion from the second case: " It is to be observed that the Privy Council has said that the proof of the existence of a joint family does not lead to the presumption that property held by any member is joint, and the burden rests upon any one asserting that any type of property is joint to establish the fact. But where it is established that the family possessed some joint property which from its nature and relative value may have formed the nucleus, from which the property in question may have been acquired, the burden shifts to the party alleging self-acquisition to establish affirmatively that the property was acquired without the aid of the joint family property.
